source: Motion of the Center of Mass
With no outside force, a system's center of mass keeps moving at a steady velocity.
Students think an explosion changes the path of the center of mass.
The center of mass of a system is its mass-weighted average position. It turns out to move in the simplest way possible, and that gives a second view of momentum conservation.

Take two objects. Their center of mass is at $x_{\text{cm}} = \dfrac{m_1x_1 + m_2x_2}{m_1 + m_2}$. In a short time each object moves $v\Delta t$, so the center of mass moves with velocity $$v_{\text{cm}} = \frac{m_1v_1 + m_2v_2}{m_1 + m_2} = \frac{p_{\text{tot}}}{M}.$$ If the total momentum is constant, so is $v_{\text{cm}}$. More generally, $\Sigma F_{\text{ext}} = M a_{\text{cm}}$: only outside forces can change how the center of mass moves.

The center of mass moves as if all the mass were there and every outside force acted on it. With no net outside force, it moves in a straight line at constant speed (or stays at rest), no matter how the parts collide, push apart or explode.
The gliders crash and change speed, but their center of mass never notices.
Worked examples
A $3.0\ \text{kg}$ glider moves right at $1.2\ \text{m/s}$ and a $1.0\ \text{kg}$ glider moves left at $0.80\ \text{m/s}$. Find $v_{\text{cm}}$.
Velocity of the center of mass
$0.70\ \text{m/s}$ right
$v_{\text{cm}} = \dfrac{2.8}{4.0} = 0.70\ \text{m/s}$ to the right, before and after they collide.
A $60\ \text{kg}$ person walks $4.0\ \text{m}$ along a $140\ \text{kg}$ raft floating at rest. How far does the raft move?
Walking on a raft
$1.2\ \text{m}$ backward
Person plus raft start at rest with no outside horizontal force (ignore water drag), so the center of mass stays put: $60\,\Delta x_p + 140\,\Delta x_r = 0$.
She moves $4.0\ \text{m}$ relative to the raft: $\Delta x_p = \Delta x_r + 4.0$.
$60(\Delta x_r + 4.0) + 140\,\Delta x_r = 0$, so $\Delta x_r = -\dfrac{240}{200} = -1.2\ \text{m}$: backward $1.2\ \text{m}$.
A firework shell would land $100\ \text{m}$ from its launch point. At the top it bursts into two equal pieces; one stops and falls straight down. Where does the other land?
A shell that bursts
$150\ \text{m}$ from the launch point
The burst is internal, so the center of mass still lands at $100\ \text{m}$.
The top is halfway, so the first piece lands at $50\ \text{m}$. Both pieces start falling from the same height with no vertical speed, so they land together.

Thinking an explosion changes the path of the center of mass. The explosion's forces are internal pairs, so they cancel in $\Sigma F_{\text{ext}}$. Only gravity (an outside force) acts before and after, so the center of mass keeps its parabola. Check: the mass-weighted average of the pieces' landing points (if they land at the same time) is where the unexploded shell would have landed.
